sections.section_title: The Remedy for Sin and the Scope of Atonement
sections.summary: The neutral reading found that when sin occurs, the community has Jesus Christ the righteous as an advocate (parakletos) before the Father, and that Jesus himself is the propitiation (hilasmos) for sins -- not for the community's sins only but for the whole world.
sections.relevance: The provision of an ongoing advocate before the Father and a propitiation whose scope extends to the entire world provides a foundation that could support permanence: the believer's sin is addressed by Christ's continuous intercession and by an atonement of universal sufficiency. The advocate's standing depends on his own righteousness ('Jesus Christ the righteous'), not on the believer's merit. However, the neutral reading also noted that the author frames this provision not as a license to continue sinning ('I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin') but as a remedy that exists within the context of the believer's pursuit of holiness.
key_phrases: we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous
he himself is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the whole world
I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin

sections.section_title: The Test of Genuine Knowledge -- Obedience
sections.summary: The neutral reading found that genuine knowledge of God is demonstrated by keeping his commandments, that claiming to know God while not keeping the commandments makes a person a liar in whom truth does not dwell, and that claiming to abide in Christ creates an obligation to walk as Christ walked.
sections.relevance: The passage establishes that the believer's claimed standing before God is validated or invalidated by observable conduct. 'The one who says I have come to know him and does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in this person.' The test is behavioral: position is verified by practice. The obligation to 'walk in the same way that one walked' makes the believer's standing contingent on correspondence between profession and conduct. The love of God is 'perfected' (brought to its intended goal) in the person who keeps God's word, implying that failure to keep the word leaves the love of God unrealized.
key_phrases: the one who says I have come to know him and does not keep his commandments is a liar
by this we know that we are in him
the one who says he abides in him ought himself to walk in the same way that one walked

sections.section_title: The Commandment -- Old and New -- and the Love Test
sections.summary: The neutral reading found that the commandment to love is both old (received from the beginning) and new (being realized in the era where the true light is shining), and that hating a brother while claiming to be in the light reveals that one has been in darkness all along, while loving one's brother demonstrates genuine abiding in the light.
sections.relevance: The passage makes the believer's location -- in light or in darkness -- contingent on whether they love or hate their brother. 'The one who hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.' The blinding is described as already accomplished (aorist tense), suggesting that hatred has already done its damage to the person's spiritual perception. The presence or absence of love for fellow believers is not an optional supplement to faith but the criterion that determines whether one is actually in the light.
key_phrases: the one who says he is in the light and hates his brother is in the darkness until now
the one who loves his brother abides in the light
the one who hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness, and does not know where he is going

sections.section_title: The Author's Reassurance of the Community
sections.summary: The neutral reading found that the author pauses between stern tests to reassure the community with six affirmations: their sins have been forgiven for his name's sake, they know the Father, they know the one from the beginning, they are strong, the word of God abides in them, and they have overcome the evil one.
sections.relevance: The passage provides a significant foundation for assurance of standing. The affirmations are stated as present realities, not merely future hopes: sins have been forgiven (perfect tense), they have overcome the evil one (perfect tense), the word of God abides in them (present tense). The basis of forgiveness is external to the believer -- 'for his name's sake' -- rooting the assurance in Christ's identity rather than in the community's performance. The neutral reading noted that this passage serves to give the community 'ground to stand on' between the author's diagnostic tests, affirming that the tests are meant to confirm their confidence, not destroy it.
key_phrases: your sins have been forgiven you for his name's sake
you know him who is from the beginning
you have overcome the evil one
the word of God abides in you

sections.section_title: The Warning Against Loving the World
sections.summary: The neutral reading found that love for the world and love for the Father are mutually exclusive, that all that is in the world (the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life) is not from the Father but from the world, and that the world is passing away while the one who does God's will abides forever.
sections.relevance: The passage presents a binary that bears on the question: 'If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.' The two loves are mutually exclusive -- one cannot possess both simultaneously. The contrast between what is temporary (the world and its desires) and what is permanent (the one who does God's will) ties eschatological destiny to present conduct. The person who does God's will 'abides forever' (menei eis ton aiona), while the world and its desires are 'passing away.' The implication is that the believer's permanent standing depends on doing God's will rather than aligning with the world's values.
key_phrases: if anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him
the world is passing away along with its desires
the one who does the will of God abides forever

sections.section_title: The Crisis of the Community -- False Teachers and the Denial of Christ
sections.summary: The neutral reading found that those who departed the community by denying that Jesus is the Christ were interpreted by the author as never having genuinely belonged: 'if they had been of us, they would have remained with us; but they went out, so that it would be shown that they all are not of us.'
sections.relevance: This passage is conventionally cited to support permanence: genuine believers always remain, and departure reveals that the person was never genuinely part of the community. The neutral reading supports this at face value -- the author does interpret departure as evidence that genuine belonging was absent. The contrary-to-fact conditional ('if they had been of us, they would have remained with us') states that true belonging would have produced remaining. However, the neutral reading also noted that this is the author's interpretation of a specific historical event (the departure of christological heretics), and that the broader letter context includes imperative commands to 'abide' (2:24, 2:27, 2:28), which would be unnecessary if abiding were guaranteed. The passage is the author's pastoral reading of a specific departure, and its extension to a universal principle about the impossibility of genuine believers departing requires caution.
key_phrases: they went out from us, but they were not of us
if they had been of us, they would have remained with us
they went out, so that it would be shown that they all are not of us

sections.section_title: The Safeguard -- Let What You Heard from the Beginning Remain in You
sections.summary: The neutral reading found that the remedy for false teaching is remaining anchored to the original apostolic message, that the anointing (the Spirit) already abides in the community and teaches them about all things, and that the promise connected to remaining is eternal life.
sections.relevance: The passage affirms the sufficiency and permanence of what the community already possesses: the original message, the anointing (Spirit), and the promise of eternal life. The anointing 'abides in you' (present indicative) -- stated as a fact, not an imperative. The community already has what they need; they do not depend on the departed teachers. The connection between abiding in the message and abiding in the Son and Father could support permanence: what God has given (the anointing) remains. However, the passage also contains conditional language: 'IF what you heard from the beginning abides in you, you also WILL abide in the Son and in the Father' -- making the relational result contingent on the message continuing to reside in them.
key_phrases: let that abide in you which you heard from the beginning
if what you heard from the beginning abides in you, you also will abide in the Son and in the Father
the anointing which you received from him abides in you

sections.section_title: Abiding, Confidence, and the Test of Righteousness
sections.summary: The neutral reading found that the author commands the community to abide in Christ so that at his appearing they may have confidence rather than shrink away in shame, and that the practice of righteousness is the evidence of having been born of God.
sections.relevance: The imperative 'abide in him' (menete en auto) implies that abiding is something the audience must actively do and could fail to do. The two possible outcomes at Christ's appearing -- confidence (parrhesia) or shame (aischyne) -- are determined by whether the person has abided. The passage presents two possible eschatological outcomes for those within the community, depending on their conduct. If abiding were automatic or guaranteed, the command would be unnecessary and the warning of shame would be hollow. The connection between practicing righteousness and being born of God (v. 29) also establishes that divine parentage is evidenced by conduct, not merely by profession.
key_phrases: abide in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not shrink away from him in shame at his coming
everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him
